title.zh: 以芬娜芭爾之名挑起的「女子之戰」

region.en: North of the Tain route, Co. Monaghan, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭莫納亨郡奪牛記行軍路（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tain Bo Cuailnge (LU recension), trans. L. Winifred Faraday (1904)

source.work: L. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #21557

summary.en: Cuchulainn sends his charioteer to Rochad Mac Fatheman of Ulster to come to his help; but Findabair loves Rochad, fairest of the Ulstermen, and she meets him by proxy in a horseman's shape: 'I have come from Findabair to meet you, that you come to speak with her.' The seven kings of the host, promised Findabair by Medb, lie in wait and Rochad slays a hundred of them at a time; the promise of the girl, made seven times over as a bribe, has raised a private war inside Meave's camp — the woman-fight by which the Tain's own bride-price logic devours it.
summary.zh: 庫丘林遣車伕召阿爾斯特的羅夏德前來相助；然芬娜芭爾鍾情於這位阿爾斯特最美的戰士，竟化身騎手傳話：「我奉芬娜芭爾之命來請你一見。」大軍中七位國王皆被梅芙許諾芬娜芭爾為酬，設伏相截；羅夏德一次斬殺百人。同一女子七次許諾的聘禮謊言，在梅芙營中釀成內戰——「女子之戰」反噬了《奪牛記》自己的贖金邏輯。

sensitivity.note: The woman-fight (ban-chath) is the LU's satiric name for the melee the promise of Findabair raises; Findabair as bride-bait recurs through the whole Tain (findabair promised to Nacrantal, to Fer Diad, to Loch), making her the cycle's currency. Pin symbolic on the route.

passages.text: Cuchulainn sent his charioteer to Rochad Mac Fatheman of Ulster, that he should come to his help. Now it happened that Findabair loved Rochad, for he was the fairest of the warriors among the Ulstermen at that time. The man goes to Rochad and told him to come. Rochad comes from the north with a hundred men. 'Rochad Mac Fatheman,' said he, 'and it is to help Cuchulainn he comes.' 'I have come from Findabair to meet you, that you come to speak with her,' said the horseman.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

passages.text: It was promised to him that Findabair should be given to him, and he returned from them then. So that that is Rochad's Woman-fight. And the seven kings who had been promised Findabair by Medb lay in wait for Rochad, and Rochad slew a hundred of their men at a time; and the promise made seven times over as a bribe raised a private war inside the camp of Meave, so that the bride-price logic of the raid devoured the raid itself.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

title.en: Cuchulainn and Findabair Make the Terms
title.zh: 庫丘林與芬娜芭爾議定條款

region.en: Tara of the Cattle-raid camp, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭奪牛記營地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tain Bo Cuailnge (LU recension), trans. L. Winifred Faraday (1904)

source.work: L. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #21557

summary.en: 'Let an offer go to him, that Findabair will be given to him,' says Ailill — and Cuchulainn, meeting the king's daughter by the ford, agrees to hold the host back for food and a champion a day, until the Ulstermen are cured. The maiden herself is made the guarantee of the truce that her own value has strained; the terms are broken within the day, and the host learns that the boy will not be bought with the girl he does not want.
summary.zh: 埃利爾提議：「向他許諾芬娜芭爾。」庫丘林與公主在渡口相會，允諾只要每日供食並遣一名勇士對決，便不襲擾大軍，直至阿爾斯特人痊愈。這位少女成了由她自己價值所繃緊的停戰擔保；條款當日即被撕毀，大軍也明白了：他們的少年戰士不會為他並不需要的姑娘所收買。

sensitivity.note: The meeting of Cuchulainn and Findabair (LU) sets the formal terms — daily champion and food — that structure the middle Tain; the breach-of-truce motif is the cycle's engine (compare the Fergus securities). Pin symbolic.

passages.text: 'Let an offer go to him,' said Ailill, 'that Findabair will be given to him, and a chariot, and the equipment of a chariot, and a maiden of the Connaughtmen with her.' And the maiden goes to Cuchulainn by the ford, and they make the terms between them: that he should not harass the host if he were supplied daily with food, and with a champion to meet him in single combat.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

passages.text: The terms were made with him then, that he should have his food and his champion daily until the Ulstermen were cured of their sickness, and Findabair herself was the pledge of it; but the terms were broken within the day, for Meave sent men against him beyond the champion of the day; and the host learned that the boy would not be bought with the girl he did not want, and that a champion a day must pay for every breach.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

title.en: The Two Bulls Fight at Tarbga

region.en: Tarbga in Mag Ai, Co. Roscommon, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭羅斯康芒郡阿伊平原塔爾加

texts.period: Tain Bo Cuailnge (YBL recension ending), trans. L. Winifred Faraday (1904)

source.work: L. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #21557

summary.en: Routed, Meave blames Fergus — 'faults meet here to-day' — and his answer is the herding-law jibe: it is customary to every herd which a mare precedes. The Bull is driven home that morning and meets the White-horned at Tarbga in Mag Ai, where every man who escaped the battle watches only the two Bulls fighting. The Dun of Cualnge lighted on the horn of the other for a day and a night till Fergus plied the rod; the horn sprang to the Mountain of the Horn; and the conquering bull carries the loin and shoulder-blade and liver of the other on his horns from loch to loch, roaring through all the province, till he dies between Ulster and Iveagh at Druim Tairb. Ailill and Medb make peace, and for seven years after there is no wounding of men between them.
summary.zh: 潰敗後，梅芙怪罪費爾古斯——「今日你我各有過失」——他以牧群之律回敬：「母馬領群的牧群，向來如此。」當晨褐牛被驅回，於阿伊平原塔爾加與白角牛相遇，戰場脫生者皆屏息觀牛。庫爾涅褐牛之足踩住對方牛角一日一夜，費爾古斯以棍催其收足，角應聲彈上「牛角山」。勝牛角挑敵牛腰肉、肩胛與肝，逐湖而飲，吼聲震徹全省，最終死於阿爾斯特與伊威之間的德魯姆·塔爾布。埃利爾與梅芙議和，此後七年，兩族刀兵不入。

sensitivity.note: The bull-fight finale is the Tain's dindsenchas engine (Sliab n-Adarca, Ath Luain, Etan Tairb, Druim Tairb are all named from the bull's journey) — the epic's place-name charter; the seven-year peace after is the corpus's post-epic reset. Pin is the traditional Tarbga site.

passages.text: When the battle was broken, then said Medb to Fergus: 'Faults and meet here to-day, O Fergus.' 'It is customary to every herd which a mare precedes; after a woman who has ill consulted their interest.' They take away the Bull then in that morning of the battle, so that he met the White-horned at Tarbga in Mag Ai; every one who escaped in the fight was intent on nothing but beholding the two Bulls fighting. Bricriu Poison-tongue came with the rest then to see the combat of the Bulls; the two Bulls went in fighting over Bricriu, so that he died therefrom. That is the Death of Bricriu.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, YBL ending; not verbatim.

passages.text: The foot of the Dun of Cualnge lighted on the horn of the other; for a day and a night he did not draw his foot towards him, till Fergus incited him and plied a rod along his body: 'Twere no good luck that this combative old calf which has been brought here should leave the honour of clan and race. Therewith he drew his foot to him so that his leg was broken, and the horn sprang from the other, and was in the mountain by him; it was Sliab n-Adarca, the Mountain of the Horn, afterwards.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, YBL ending; not verbatim.

passages.text: He carried them then a journey of a day and a night, till he lighted in the loch which is by Cruachan, and he came to Cruachan out of it with the loin and the shoulder-blade and the liver of the other on his horns. He drank a draught in Findlethe; he drank another draught in Ath Luain; he gave forth his roar on Iraird Chuillend, and it was heard through all the province; there the liver of the other fell from his horns, hence is Tromma; and he went till he died between Ulster and Iveagh at Druim Tairb. Ailill and Medb made peace with the Ulstermen and with Cuchulainn; for seven years after there was no wounding of men between them. Findabair stayed with Cuchulainn, and the Connaughtmen went to their country, and the Ulstermen to Emain Macha with their great triumph. Finit, amen.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, YBL ending; not verbatim.
